# Mortar documentation map

Mortar writes version-control history for teams of coding agents, with plain
git. It makes the folders agents work in, saves their work, joins a request to
its zone, squashes a zone's work, lands it, and guards the branches that hold
proven code. It runs `git` as a program and links no git library. The command
is `mr`; `mortar` is the long name for the same program. This file routes
humans and AI agents to the maintained sources.

## Start here

- Product overview, install, a first run, every verb: README.md
- What an AI should read first, and the rules for an agent: AI_START_HERE.md
- Documentation index, by reader and by topic: docs/README.md
- What the guard protects and what it does not: SECURITY.md
- Build, test and layout of the code: CONTRIBUTING.md
- What each version does: CHANGELOG.md
- License (MIT): LICENSE

## The program is a source

- `mr help` lists every verb with one line each.
- `mr help <verb>` and `mr <verb> --help` print one verb's usage.
- A command line that cannot be read exits 4, lists the verbs, and gives as its
  next step the verb's usage line when the verb is known, or the list of verbs
  when it is not.
- Every verb's last line is `next: <one step>`. `--version` prints its one line only, and the guard hook prints nothing when it allows a move.
- `--json` on any verb prints one JSON object on one line: verb, ok, outcome,
  exit, next, lines, owner, then the verb's own fields. `--version --json`
  prints verb, ok, version and commit; `mortar --json guard-hook` prints
  nothing when it allows a move.

When a document and the program disagree, the program is right.

## The verbs

Agent verbs, run inside a request folder, with no folder argument and no
`--actor`:

- `mr status`
- `mr save "<sentence>"`
- `mr join`
- `mr resolve`
- `mr need <path>`
- `mr undo`

Set-up and folder verbs, run by a harness or a person, with `--actor <name>`:

- `mr init --origin <branch> --integration <branch> --remote <name> [--zone <zone>=<path>[,<path>...]]...`
- `mr guard install`, `mr guard status`
- `mr folder zone <zone> <path> [--start <commit>]`
- `mr folder request <zone> <request> <path> --paths <path>...`
- `mr folder remove <path>`
- `mr folder attempts <n> <dir>`, `mr folder keep <k>`, `mr folder drop`
- `mr snapshot`, `mr overlap <zone>`, `mr disk`, `mr sweep [--idle-days <n>] [--ref <full ref name>]...`
- `mr restore <op id> <full ref name>...`

Landing verbs, with `--actor <name>`:

- `mr squash <zone>`
- `mr would-merge <commit or change ID>`
- `mr rereview <reviewed commit> <new commit>`
- `mr land <commit>`
- `mr back-out`
- `mr publish`
- `mr after-publish <zone> [--move <zone>]...`
- `mr backup`, `mr restore-backup <host>`
- `mr bisect <last pass> <failed> --timeout <seconds> -- <command>...`

Read only, no `--actor` needed:

- `mr log [--ref <full ref name>] [--actor <name>] [--key <operation key>]`

Run by git's hooks, never by hand:

- `mortar guard-hook`

Program verbs:

- `mortar install`, `mortar uninstall`, `mortar --version`, `mr help [<verb>]`

## Exit codes

- 0: done, or already done (a repeat of a finished command)
- 1: refused; the text says why, who owns the thing in the way, and what to do
- 2: conflict; the files are listed
- 3: busy; a lock is held, or a branch or snapshot ref moved while mr save
  or mr snapshot ran (repeat later); or a landing is in flight (finish it
  first with mr publish or mr back-out)
- 4: usage
- 5: failure; git or the disk failed. The report says what happened, and its
  next line says what to do: usually the same command again, sometimes a path
  to remove by hand first.

## Where Mortar keeps things

- Config: `<git common dir>/mortar/config.json`
- Operation log: `<git common dir>/mortar/oplog.jsonl`
- Locks: `<git common dir>/mortar/locks/`
- Guard config and landing in flight: `<git common dir>/mortar/guard.json`, `<git common dir>/mortar/landing.json`
- A folder's record and a paused join: `mortar-folder.json` and `mortar-join.json` in the worktree's own git dir
- Branches: `zone/<zone>`, `req/<zone>/<request>`, `try/<zone>/<request>/<k>`
- Hidden refs: `refs/mortar/snap/<zone>/<request>`, `refs/mortar/trysnap/<zone>/<request>/<k>`, `refs/mortar/squash/<zone>`

## Code map

- `crates/gitio`: the one place that runs git
- `crates/oplog`: the operation log, recovery, undo and restore, locks, change IDs
- `crates/folders`: worktrees, sparse paths, folder records, attempts, disk report, sweeps
- `crates/snapshot`: saving a folder to a commit or a hidden ref; the formatter run
- `crates/join`: joining a request to its zone: replay, conflicts, resolve, overlap
- `crates/land`: squash, would-merge, re-review, land, back-out, publish, after-publish, the guard, backup, bisect
- `crates/cli`: the program: verbs, arguments, output, exit codes
- `crates/testkit`: throwaway repositories for tests

## Sibling tools

- Tessera (`ts`) reads a codebase and answers questions about it from an index.
- Temperare (`tm`) checks code against the rules a repository has chosen.

Each works alone. Mortar needs neither and calls neither.

## What Mortar is not

Not a replacement for git, not a harness that starts agents, not a test runner
or reviewer, not a hosting or pull-request tool, not a security boundary, and
not for Windows.

## Version note

This is version 0.2.0. Mortar is built from source.
The command line, the `--json` fields and the layout under `refs/mortar/` may
still change before 1.0.
